about: Lesson A4 (a04-retail-tariffs), wave W3, 2026-11-03. Prairie Town is fictional: its customers, their hourly use, the utility's unit costs, the four tariffs and the large load are illustrative. The day's prices come from the town's own dispatch on 9 June 2025 (real Southwest Power Pool shapes from EIA-930 in town_year.json, scaled as lesson 9 does: demand = shape x 450 MW, wind = shape x 150 MW, sun = shape x 200 MW, whole MW; the town's 100 MW always-on plant runs flat; then wind and sun, the combined-cycle plant at $40/MWh, the peaker at $100/MWh). The rooftop array follows the same real solar shape. A month is 30 days like this one. Every number on the page is checked by _tests/learn/test_a04-retail-tariffs.js.

day.why: Lesson 9's day and CF6's: nine hours of spare midday sun (08:00-17:00) and an evening that needs the peaker (20:00-23:00).

customers.name: Renter in an apartment
customers.note: No car, no solar; air conditioning in the evening.

customers.name: Home with rooftop solar and an EV
customers.note: A larger house with central air, a 4 kW rooftop array and a 7 kW car charger.

customers.name: Small factory
customers.note: Two shifts, 06:00 to 22:00, and a 200 kW batch process that runs two hours a day.

home.label: Homes
home.mixNote: For setting prices, Prairie Town's homes are taken as nine like the renter for each one like the solar and EV home.

business.label: Businesses
business.mixNote: The factory stands for its class.

costs.note: Illustrative unit costs a month: $15 per kW drawn in the town's tightest hour (plants and lines are sized for hours like it), $6 per kW of the customer's own busiest hour (the local transformer and service line), and the class's meter and billing cost; energy is the town's running cost in each hour.

parts.label: Plants for the town's tightest hour
Local wires for the customer's busiest hour

tariffs.name: Time-of-use
tariffs.pays: kWh at a higher price from 16:00 to 21:00

tariffs.name: Demand charge
tariffs.pays: kWh at a low price, plus each kW of the month's busiest hour
tariffs.rewards: a flatter day: a lower busiest hour

tariffs.name: Real-time
tariffs.pays: each kWh at the town's price that hour, plus a plant-and-wire charge per kWh

tariffNote: Illustrative tariffs, each set so that a class pays its total cost before anyone changes what they do. In all four, a kWh sent back earns what a kWh bought costs in that hour (net metering).

scarcity.label: five evenings at $2,000 per MWh, 20:00 to 23:00

large.note: Illustrative: a 100 MW data center (a large load) with its own tariff; the utility's upgrades built to serve it cost $15M a year, recovered by a demand charge on its billing demand. Billing demand = the greater of its highest hourly demand in the month and the minimum share of its contract. Assumed: what it does not pay is recovered from the utility's other customers.

facts.what: Average U.S. residential electricity price in 2025 (commercial 13.37¢, industrial 8.51¢).
Share of U.S. electricity meters that were advanced meters in December 2023 (128.4 of 167.2 million). Time-of-use needs use split by price period; real-time pricing needs hourly readings.
facts.source: FERC staff, 2025 Assessment of Demand Response and Advanced Metering, p. 2 and Table 2-1, p. 4 (EIA data)

facts.what: Across 55 large-load tariffs reviewed, the median minimum billing demand was 80% of contract demand; the median minimum contract rose from 5 years (tariffs proposed before 2025) to 12 years (since 2025).
facts.source: Berkeley Lab and The Brattle Group, Electricity Rate Designs for Large Loads, 2026 Update, pp. 2, 4, 5
